content.text: Irving Copi's system has two kinds of rules.

content.definition: Work one way, on whole lines. Modus tollens: from P → Q and ¬Q, infer ¬P.
Swap equivalent forms in either direction, even inside a line. De Morgan: ¬(P ∧ Q) becomes ¬P ∨ ¬Q.

examples.title: Rules of inference
lines: Hypothetical syllogism: P → Q, Q → R, so P → R
Disjunctive syllogism: P ∨ Q, ¬P, so Q

examples.title: Rules of replacement
lines: De Morgan: ¬(P ∧ Q) is equivalent to ¬P ∨ ¬Q
Double negation: ¬¬P is equivalent to P
Contraposition: P → Q is equivalent to ¬Q → ¬P

question.prompt: How do rules of replacement differ from rules of inference?
options: They swap equivalent forms either way, even inside a line
question.hint: Can you apply modus ponens to part of a line?
question.explanation: Rules of inference apply one way to whole lines. Rules of replacement swap equivalent forms in either direction, anywhere in a line.
